extracted.intended_audience: general readers, film viewers, and scholars of media/science communication interested in Don't Look Up
extracted.subtask_description: Encyclopedic thematic analysis of the film Don't Look Up, focusing on how it depicts science communication, politics, gender, symbolism, and cultural perspectives. Useful for readers and scholars evaluating the film's themes and social commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: The topic of science communication
rubrics_metrics.description: The film 'revolves around Mindy and Dibiasky, two scientists, struggling to share the news of their discovery with politicians, talk show hosts, and civilians who are ignorant about the scientific facts of humanity's impending destruction by Comet Dibiasky.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scholars analyze and critique the portrayal: Niels G. Mede writes the film 'depicts sharp partisan divides, strong affective polarization, high distrust toward science within certain social milieus, and pronounced news media sensationalism.' Use this dimension to evaluate how accurately and deeply the film represents the social dynamics of science communication (public ignorance, political resistance, media sensationalism). Examples: scenes of failed press briefings and TV appearances illustrating those dynamics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Americentrism
rubrics_metrics.description: The film 'fails to center any marginalized voices, continuing to privilege global north perspectives, even as these are satirised.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Julie Doyle's critique: although the film critiques existing structures it 'does not imagine an alternative set of realities, nor explain the comet's cause.' Use this as a criterion to judge whose perspectives the film centers or excludes, and whether it offers alternatives or broader global-contextualized explanation. Related note: 'climate communication needs to keep in place both climate mitigation and adaptation, making the historical and structural inequalities of capitalism and colonialism the interconnected stories of both.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Media training for scientists
rubrics_metrics.description: The film raises media training as a solution to failed science communication (e.g., Chief Editor proposes media training to Mindy before a show).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Samer Angelone: 'The style that scientists use to communicate science to peer scientists is mostly objective, complex, and full of technical jargon, which is difficult for the general public to connect to—even if it is in the same language.' Evaluate the film on whether it shows media training as practical, caricatured, or insufficient. Example practices shown: advice to 'keep it simple' or frame scientific facts as a story; consider whether media training is portrayed as meaningful mitigation or merely performative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Storytelling as a mitigation strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The film also illustrates that storytelling can be a promising strategy to mitigate these reservations ... showing how Mindy is advised before a TV interview that he is "just telling a story" and must "keep it simple."'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat storytelling as an explicit communicative technique promoted in the film: assess how the film represents storytelling's potential and limits in persuading skeptical publics. Use this to evaluate narrative choices within the film itself (e.g., how scientists' messages are reshaped for TV, and whether simplification aids or distorts scientific truth).

rubrics_metrics.name: Gendered emotions in scientific communication
rubrics_metrics.description: Gendered discourse on emotions and mental health affects public reaction to Mindy and Dibiasky's media appearances; 'Gendered norms affect Mindy and Dibiasky's public credibility and the mitigatory comet actions they promote.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Julie Doyle's analysis: after an emotional outburst Mindy is 'recuperated through processes of celebritisation ... hailed as a "sexy" scientist offering rational and calm advice' while Dibiasky is 'discredited and side-lined from rational public commentary through (climate) memes.' Use this criterion to evaluate how the film depicts gendered expectations about emotion and credibility, and whether it reinforces or critiques double standards in public reception of male vs female scientists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation of populism and anti‑science rhetoric
rubrics_metrics.description: The film 'references the affinity of anti-science resentment and populism, showing how President Orlean and her team slander Mindy and Dibiasky using populist rhetoric.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate portrayals of political actors and rhetoric: how does the film depict political manipulation, slander, and the weaponization of populist messaging against scientific expertise? Consider scenes of the Oval Office, political advisors, and media collusion as examples of this dimension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of historic figures and Easter eggs as symbolic commentary
rubrics_metrics.description: Throughout the film many historic figures from science and politics appear as visual references (e.g., a figure of Carl Sagan on Dibiasky's desk, a painting of George W. Bush, an Oval Office portrait of Andrew Jackson).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Samer Angelone notes Sagan 'was an upholder of scientific credibility and communication.' Use the presence and juxtaposition of these easter eggs to assess the film's intertextual commentary on scientific authority, political history, and cultural memory. Consider how such references bolster or complicate the film's satire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious/Last Supper imagery at the ending
rubrics_metrics.description: The film ends with a scene that reflects the Last Supper: Dr. Mindy, his family, Kate, Yule, and Teddy sit around a dinner table, engage in a hand-held prayer spoken by Yule, followed by a kiss and then the comet destroys Earth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as a criterion for evaluating the film's symbolic and tonal choices: the invocation of religious ritual and communal intimacy immediately before annihilation suggests commentary on denial, ritualized comfort, or resignation. Assess whether the film's final imagery enhances its satirical argument or undermines it by tonal dissonance.
